canonical_statement: Erdos problem 850 (erdosproblems.com/850, OPEN), Lean target erdos_850: answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ x y : ℕ, x ≠ y ∧ x.primeFactors = y.primeFactors ∧ (x + 1).primeFactors = (y + 1).primeFactors ∧ (x + 2).primeFactors = (y + 2).primeFactors. Verbatim source statement: "Can there exist two distinct integers $x$ and $y$ such that $x,y$ have the same prime factors, $x+1,y+1$ have the same prime factors, and $x+2,y+2$ also have the same prime factors?" Note the formalization quantifies over ℕ (nonneg integers), not ℤ.

must_determine: the explicit pair (x, y) ∈ ℕ² with x ≠ y, verified by exact computation of all three primeFactors equalities (world-verifier check)
or a parametric infinite family with a proof valid for every member, plus at least one concrete witness
the Lean wiring: answer(true) ↔ ∃ x y, ... discharged in the correct direction
close_branch_A.statement: AFFIRMATIVE: exhibit, with a fully verified proof, two distinct natural numbers x ≠ y satisfying all three primeFactors equalities simultaneously — i.e. prove the ∃-side and set answer = true in the Lean biconditional.

must_determine: an impossibility argument covering EVERY pair x ≠ y in ℕ², with the cases x ∈ {0, 1} or y ∈ {0, 1} explicitly discharged, not silently excluded
the Lean wiring: answer(false) ↔ ∃ x y, ... discharged, i.e. a proof of ¬∃ x y, ... in the correct direction
close_branch_B.statement: NEGATIVE: prove that no two distinct natural numbers x, y satisfy the three simultaneous primeFactors equalities — i.e. prove the negation of the ∃-side over the FULL domain ℕ (all pairs including those with a coordinate in {0, 1}) and set answer = false in the Lean biconditional.

definitions: primeFactors(n) for n ∈ ℕ, n ≥ 2: the finite set of primes p with p | n (mathlib Nat.primeFactors; order irrelevant, equality is set equality)
Endpoint conventions (mathlib, must be pinned): Nat.primeFactors 0 = ∅ and Nat.primeFactors 1 = ∅. These are the Lean semantics of the formal statement and remain fixed in every reformulation.
Domain: x, y ∈ ℕ = {0, 1, 2, ...}; the quantifier ∃ x y : ℕ ranges over ALL of ℕ including 0 and 1 — no restriction to x, y ≥ 2 is licensed by the statement
Distinctness: x ≠ y as elements of ℕ, strict inequality, applied to the pair (x, y) itself (not to x+1, y+1 etc.; note x ≠ y implies x+1 ≠ y+1 and x+2 ≠ y+2 automatically)

The conjunction is over three simultaneous set equalities: primeFactors(x) = primeFactors(y), primeFactors(x+1) = primeFactors(y+1), primeFactors(x+2) = primeFactors(y+2); all three must hold for the same pair (x, y)
Quantifier order: a single existential pair (∃ x y) must satisfy all three equalities at once; there is no per-shift existential
The theorem is the biconditional answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ x y, ... : the value of `answer` is TRUE iff such a pair exists
invariants_that_must_survive_every_refor: x, y ∈ ℕ (nonnegative); no lifting to ℤ or restriction to positive integers
all THREE set equalities primeFactors(x+k) = primeFactors(y+k) for k = 0, 1, 2, simultaneously for one pair
primeFactors(0) = ∅ and primeFactors(1) = ∅ (mathlib conventions) wherever those arguments occur
primeFactors equality is set equality of primes (multiplicity ignored)
the exact quantifier structure: single ∃ x y over ℕ with a three-way conjunction; and the biconditional answer ↔ ∃-side
known_traps: empty-support vacuity: primeFactors(0) = primeFactors(1) = ∅, so any pair with coordinates in {0, 1} satisfies individual equalities vacuously — a pair matching one or two of the three shifts via ∅-support is a near-solution, not a solution; e.g. (x, y) with primeFactors(x+1) = primeFactors(y+1) = ∅ forces x+1, y+1 ∈ {0, 1}, forcing x, y ∈ {-1, 0}, so within ℕ this collapses to x = y = 0 which violates x ≠ y — verify such collapses explicitly rather than assuming them
off-by-one: the shifts are x, x+1, x+2 (not x-1, x, x+1); a pair matching at shifted indices is not a witness

multiplicity confusion: primeFactors ignores multiplicity; a pair with equal radicals but different exponents still satisfies the equalities — do not falsely reject, and conversely do not present equal-radical near-misses as different objects
biconditional direction: a close must wire answer ↔ ∃-side correctly (true for branch A, false for branch B); proving the ∃-side and then asserting answer(false), or its mirror, is a wiring failure
domain drift: working over ℤ or restricting to x, y ≥ 2 changes the problem; branch B must cover x, y ∈ {0, 1} cases explicitly
verified finite search claimed as a universal obstruction (sampled-to-universal)
coprimality confusions among x, x+1, x+2 (pairwise coprime) misused to derive false obstructions
non_results: solutions or obstructions over ℤ (negative integers) presented as settling the ℕ-quantified statement
a negative result valid only for x, y ≥ 2 (or x, y > any bound) presented as branch B, with the 0/1 cases assumed rather than discharged
a positive result for pairs agreeing at only one or two of the three shifts (x, x+1, x+2) — all three equalities are required for the same pair
radical or 'same distinct prime factors up to multiplicity' variants, or same-Ω/same-ω substitutions, in place of exact primeFactors set equality
conditional results assuming ABC, Dickson, or any comparable-strength unproved conjecture
density / almost-all statements, heuristic searches, or numerical fit without an exact witness or full impossibility proof
finite computation without a valid finite-reduction theorem covering the entire remaining infinite range
permitted_background: elementary prime factorization and unique factorization in ℕ
mathlib Nat.primeFactors API, including Nat.primeFactors 0 = ∅ and Nat.primeFactors 1 = ∅
basic gcd/coprimality facts and modular arithmetic over ℕ/ℤ
sieve-theoretic and analytic number theory already standard in the literature on the Erdős–Selfridge / consecutive-equal-radical problems (used only as proved background, not as unproved conjectures)
finite exhaustive verification ONLY when paired with a valid finite-reduction theorem covering the remaining infinite range
